Author

Justin Hamilton and Josh Rubin

Data source

IPUMS USA

Load IPUMS data

# install.packages("ipumsr")
library(ipumsr)
# NOTE: To load data, you must download both the extract's data and the DDI
# and also set the working directory to the folder with these files (or change the path below).

if (!require("ipumsr")) stop("Reading IPUMS data into R requires the ipumsr package. It can be installed using the following command: install.packages('ipumsr')")

ddi <- read_ipums_ddi("usa_00043.xml")
data <- read_ipums_micro(ddi)

Distribution of usual hours worked by gender

library(tidyverse)

data |>
  filter(AGE > 15 & WKSWORK1 > 0) |>
  mutate(
    UHRSWORK = ifelse(UHRSWORK == 99, NA, UHRSWORK)
  ) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = UHRSWORK, y = factor(SEX))) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = NA, 
    width = 0.5, 
    staplewidth = 0.4, 
    median.linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of usual hours worked by gender, 2024",
    subtitle = "Among individuals 16 years and older and worked last year",
    caption = "Source: IPUMS USA, American Community Survey (ACS) 2024 1-year estimates.\nNote: Estimates reflect unweighted results from the ACS. Bolded lines represent the median hours worked."
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = "Sex",                         
    labels = c("1" = "Male", "2" = "Female")
  ) +
  xlab("Usual hours worked per week") +
  theme_minimal()
  • Same median but male distribution is much more tightly concentrated around 40 hours
  • Females have greater variation in weekly hours worked
  • May reflect responsibilities outside of work in addition to generally being more marginally attached to workforce than males

Labor force participation rate by gender

lfpr_data <- data |>
  filter(AGE > 15 & LABFORCE != 0) |>
  mutate(
    LABFORCE = case_when(
      LABFORCE == 2 ~ 1,
      LABFORCE == 1 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA
    ),
    sex_clean = ifelse(SEX == 1, "Male", "Female")
  ) |>
  group_by(sex_clean) |>
  summarize(
    LFPR = mean(LABFORCE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(data = lfpr_data, mapping = aes(x = sex_clean, y = LFPR, fill = sex_clean)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    mapping = aes(label = scales::percent(LFPR, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.75) +
  labs(
    title = "Labor force participation rate by gender, 2024",
    subtitle = "Among individuals 16 years and older",
    caption = "Source: IPUMS USA, American Community Survey (ACS) 2024 1-year estimates.\nNote: Estimates reflect unweighted results from the ACS." 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  xlab("Sex") +
  ylab("Labor force participation rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
  • Male LFPR is over 7pp higher than female LFPR
  • Again a reflection of weaker attachment from females to the labor force than males
  • Lower female LFPR presents a potential point of deadweight loss if these individuals want to work but cannot due to barriers to employment or other circumstances

Labor force participation rate differences by marital status and gender

lfpr_gender_mar <- data |>
  filter(AGE > 15, LABFORCE != 0) |>
  mutate(
    LABFORCE = case_when(
      LABFORCE == 2 ~ 1,
      LABFORCE == 1 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA
      )
  ) |>
  group_by(SEX, MARST) |>
  summarize(lfpr = mean(LABFORCE, na.rm = TRUE))

lfpr_gender_mar |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(x = factor(MARST), y = lfpr, fill = factor(SEX)), position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Labor Force Participation Rate by Gender and Marital Status",
    subtitle = "Among individuals 16 years and older",
    x = "Marital Status",
    y = "Labor force participation rate (%)",
    fill = "Gender",
    caption = "Source: IPUMS USA, American Community Survey (ACS) 2024 1-year estimates.\nNote: Estimates reflect unweighted results from the ACS."
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(
    "1" = "Married, spouse present",
    "2" = "Married, spouse absent",
    "3" = "Separated",
    "4" = "Divorced",
    "5" = "Widowed",
    "6" = "Never married/single"
    )) +
  scale_fill_discrete(labels = c(
    "1" = "Male",
    "2" = "Female"
    )) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)
  )
  • Call attention to large gap for “Married, spouse present” but limited differences between “married, spouse absent” and “divorced”

Relationship between state education levels and labor force participation rate

state_data <- data %>%
  filter(AGE > 15, EDUC != 0, LABFORCE != 0) %>%
  mutate(
    LABFORCE = case_when(
      LABFORCE == 2 ~ 1,
      LABFORCE == 1 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA
      ),
    COLLEGE = ifelse(
      EDUC >= 7,
      1,
      0
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(STATEFIP) %>%
  summarize(
    LFPR = mean(LABFORCE, na.rm = TRUE),
    COLLEGE_PERC = mean(COLLEGE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

state_data %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = COLLEGE_PERC, y = LFPR)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = COLLEGE_PERC, y = LFPR), se = FALSE, method = "lm", color = "skyblue1") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between state share of residents with some college
    \nand state labor force participation rate",
    subtitle = "Among individuals 16 years and older",
    x = "Percentage of individuals with at least some college",
    y = "Labor force participation rate (%)",
    caption = "Source: IPUMS USA, American Community Survey (ACS) 2024 1-year estimates.\nNote: Estimates reflect unweighted results from the ACS."
  ) + 
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  theme_minimal()
  • Increasing college education is associated with increased labor force participation
  • Could be a potential policy lever (increasing college attendance) for increasing LFPR
  • Going to college –> learn about personal finance –> more likely to want a job –> increase labor force participation rate.
